front: Goal versus objective
back:
| | Goal | Objective |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Scope | Broad aim | Specific target |
| Time frame | Long term, often open-ended | A stated deadline |
| Measurable | Not directly | Yes: a figure to check against |
| Example | Improve customer service | Answer 90% of calls within two minutes by June |
mistake: Goals and objectives aren't alternatives. Each objective should serve a goal, and the goal is achieved through its objectives.

front: An objective is written so that it can be {{measured}}, and it states a {{time frame}} for achieving it.
back: Without a measure and a deadline, an organisation can't tell whether it has met the objective.

front: Why do medium and large organisations set measurable objectives as well as broad goals?
back: Many departments and staff must work towards the same aims. Objectives turn each goal into targets they can plan for, and managers can measure results to see whether the goal is being achieved.

front: How does a software development project support an organisation's goals?
back: The software is built to meet objectives that serve a goal. An online claims portal that halves claim processing time meets an objective that supports the goal of better customer service.
mistake: A project justified only by the technology ('we need an app') is weak. Link it to the goal and objective it serves.

front: How can insecure software development practices threaten an organisation's goals?
back: A breach caused by weak development practices can bring financial loss, legal penalties, disrupted services and lost customer trust. Each works directly against goals such as growth, profitability or a trusted reputation.

front: Goal or objective? 'Reduce the number of failed website logins reported to the help desk by 30% within six months.'
back: An objective. It sets a measurable target (a 30% reduction) and a time frame (six months).

front: Goal
back: A broad, long-term aim stating what an organisation wants to achieve, such as improving customer service or growing its membership. Because it usually can't be measured directly, the organisation sets objectives that work towards it.
mistake: Goals and objectives aren't interchangeable. A goal is broad and long term; an objective is a specific, measurable target with a time frame that helps achieve a goal.

front: Objective
back: A specific, measurable target with a time frame, set to help an organisation achieve one of its goals, such as cutting the time taken to process an insurance claim by 20% within a year.

front: In-house development
back: Software designed, built and maintained by the organisation's own employees, using its own equipment and processes.

front: External development
back: Software designed and built for the organisation by another company or a contractor, under a contract that sets the requirements, cost and deadline.

front: In-house versus external development
back:
| | In-house | External |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Control | Organisation sets priorities and controls the code | Shared, and set by the contract |
| Expertise | Limited to current staff | Specialist skills and experience |
| Knowledge of the organisation | Already there | Must be learned |
| Data and code | Stay inside the organisation | Shared with a third party |
| Cost | Salaries, training, equipment | Contract price, plus fees for later changes |
mistake: External development isn't automatically cheaper. Fees for changes, support and maintenance after delivery can outweigh the cost of in-house staff.

front: Why can in-house development make it easier to protect data and source code?
back: Only the organisation's own staff handle the data and code, under its own security policies, access controls and supervision. No third party needs access, so there are fewer people and systems through which data could leak.

front: When is external development likely to be the better choice?
back: When the organisation's staff lack the specialist skills needed, when the project is a one-off that doesn't justify hiring, or when the solution is needed sooner than existing staff could deliver it.

front: What security risk does external development create for an organisation's data?
back: The developer's staff may need access to personal or confidential data and to the source code. A breach at the developer, weak practices or a dishonest employee there can expose that data, and the organisation can't directly control how it is protected.
mistake: Outsourcing the work doesn't outsource the responsibility. Customers still hold the organisation that collected their data responsible when it leaks.

front: How can an organisation reduce the risks of external development?
back:
- A contract stating requirements, deadlines, cost, ownership of the code and security obligations
- A confidentiality agreement for the developer's staff
- Invented test data, with access to real data only where essential
- Its own code review and testing of what is delivered

front: Before external development starts, the contract should state who owns the {{source code}} and that it is handed over when the project ends.
back: Without the source code, even a small fix or security patch depends on the original developer, who may charge for it, refuse, or go out of business.

front: Why is communication usually easier when software is developed in-house rather than by an external team?
back: In-house developers work alongside the staff who know the business, so they can ask questions, show early versions and sort out misunderstandings as they go. An external team works through the contract and a few contact people, so requirements are more easily misunderstood, and the mistakes may not show up until the software is delivered.
mistake: Easier communication is only half a justification for building in-house. Pair it with the drawback of the external option: requirements that pass through a contract and a few contacts are easily misunderstood.

front: Vulnerability versus threat versus risk
back:
| | Meaning | Example |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Vulnerability | A weakness that could be exploited | A former developer's account is still active |
| Threat | An action, device or event that could harm data or systems, often by exploiting a weakness | The former developer, or an attacker who learns the password, logging in to change code |
| Risk | How likely harm is, combined with how severe it would be | High: the account can still change live code |
mistake: A hacker's attack is the threat, not the vulnerability. The vulnerability is the weakness the attack exploits, such as the account that was never disabled.

front: Why is it a vulnerability for development, testing and production to share one environment?
back: Untested code and developers' experiments run on the live system, so one faulty change, such as an update, can bring in bugs or vulnerabilities, corrupt real data or take the service down. Developers also end up with access to production data they don't need.
mistake: The danger comes from the change itself reaching live users untested, even an honest one. Asked about going ahead with an update in a combined environment, explain the risks of that update, not the risks of leaving software un-updated.

front: Why is writing passwords or API keys directly into source code a vulnerability?
back: Anyone who can read the code, including other staff, external developers or the public if the repository is exposed, gains those credentials. The secret also stays in earlier versions kept by version control.

front: Insider threat
back: A threat that comes from inside the organisation: an action by someone with legitimate access, such as an employee or contractor, that could harm its systems, code or data.
mistake: A phishing campaign run by outsiders isn't an insider threat just because an employee clicks the link. An insider threat comes from someone with legitimate access, such as a developer whose change to the development environment's settings makes its code and data public.

front: Why is testing with copies of real personal data a risk?
back: Test environments usually have weaker controls and more people with access than production. Real personal data there can be seen by staff who don't need it, or leaked if the test environment is breached.

front: Why do unpatched development tools and third-party libraries put an organisation at risk?
back: Security fixes are usually published with a description of the flaw they fix, so attackers know what to look for in systems that haven't been updated. A flaw in a widely used library can affect every program built with it.

front: Why is it a risk for several developers to share one login account?
back: No action can be traced to one person, so mistakes and misuse can't be investigated. The password also spreads further, and access can't be removed from one person, such as someone who leaves, without changing it for everyone.

front: Risk
back: The chance that a threat will exploit a vulnerability, considered together with how much harm it would cause. Rating each one by likelihood and impact lets a management plan deal with the most serious first and propose controls for them.
mistake: Risk isn't the same as a threat. A threat is what could cause harm; risk combines how likely that harm is with how severe it would be, so an unlikely threat with a severe impact can still be a high risk.

front: Vulnerability
back: A weakness in a system, program, process or development environment that a threat could exploit to cause harm, such as unpatched software, an administrator password shared by the whole team, or development, testing and production combined in one environment.
mistake: A vulnerability is the weakness itself. A threat is what might exploit it, and risk combines how likely that is with how much harm it would cause.

front: How can malware put a development environment at risk?
back: Malware can reach a developer's computer or the build server through a downloaded tool, an infected library or an email attachment. It can steal the source code and any passwords or keys stored there, slip malicious code into the program being built so that it reaches every user, or encrypt the code and data (ransomware) so that development stops.
mistake: Malware in a development environment doesn't harm only one computer. Code it changes can be released to every customer who installs the software.

front: Cyber security incident
back: An unwanted or unexpected event that has harmed, or is likely to harm, an organisation's systems, code or data, such as a ransomware attack, a data breach or someone getting into the code repository without authorisation. The risk can outlast the event: stolen passwords and leaked source code can be used in later attacks.
mistake: An incident is the event itself, not the weakness behind it. An unpatched build server is a vulnerability; an attack that uses it to copy the source code is a cyber security incident.

front: What makes code review practices ineffective, and why is that a vulnerability?
back: Reviews that are optional or skipped under deadline pressure, authors approving their own changes, code (including AI-generated code) approved without being read, or reviewers who don't look for security problems such as hard-coded passwords. Flaws, and malicious code added by an insider or an attacker, can then reach the live software unnoticed.
mistake: Having a review step on paper isn't enough. If changes can be merged without one, or approved without being read, the code is effectively unreviewed.

front: Physical versus software security controls
back:
| | Physical controls | Software controls |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Protect | Premises, hardware and storage media | Systems, code and data, through programs and settings |
| Examples | Locked server rooms, swipe-card entry, CCTV, locked storage for backup drives | Authentication, access permissions, encryption, version control, patching |
mistake: Physical controls still matter when data is digital. A thief who takes a laptop or backup drive can read its data directly, without logging in, unless the data is encrypted.

front: How does robust identity and access management protect a development environment?
back: It confirms each developer's identity when they log in to their own account, so only authorised people reach the code. It then limits each account to the code, modules and data that person's duties need, with administrator rights only for the few who need them, and changes access as soon as someone changes role or leaves.
mistake: Answers about protecting confidential customer data miss the point: that data shouldn't be in a development environment at all. There, identity and access management protects the code and development data by authenticating developers and limiting what each can reach.

front: Authentication versus authorisation
back:
| | Authentication | Authorisation |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Question | Who are you? | What may you do? |
| How | Password, security key, fingerprint | Permissions or roles attached to the account |
| Example | A developer logs in with a password and a code | That developer may change test code but not release to production |

Authentication happens first.
mistake: Logging in doesn't decide what a user can do. A correctly authenticated user should still get only the permissions their role needs.

front: Authentication factors fall into three main categories: something you {{know}}, something you {{have}} and something you {{are}}.
back: A password or PIN is known; a phone or security key is had; a fingerprint or face (a biometric) is what you are.

front: How does version control act as a security control in software development?
back: It records every change with who made it and when, so unauthorised or faulty changes can be traced and reviewed, everyone works from the current version, and the code can be rolled back to a working version when errors can't be fixed.
mistake: Version control isn't a backup. It keeps the code's history so changes can be traced and undone; protecting data against loss is the job of backups.

front: Why is a code review a security control?
back: A second developer examines code before it is merged. This catches vulnerabilities the author missed, such as a hard-coded password or missing validation, and makes it harder for anyone to slip in malicious code unnoticed.

front: Encryption at rest versus encryption in transit
back:
| | At rest | In transit |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Protects | Stored data: databases, backups, laptops | Data moving across a network |
| Guards against | A stolen or copied drive being read | Data being intercepted on the way |
mistake: Encryption doesn't stop data being copied or intercepted; it makes the copy unreadable without the key. That is why sensitive data an application stores should be encrypted: a backup only guards against losing it.

front: Authentication
back: Confirming that a user or device really is who or what it claims to be before access is given, using something the user knows (a password), has (a phone or security key) or is (a fingerprint). It is part of the security characteristic of user experience: login and logout features show users that their data is protected.
mistake: Authentication confirms identity; it doesn't decide what the user may do. Authorisation is the separate step that sets what an identified user can access.

front: Regular updates and patches to software
back: A security control: promptly installing the fixes (patches) and updates that vendors release for software, including operating systems, applications, libraries and development tools. Each patch corrects bugs or closes a known vulnerability that attackers may already be trying to exploit in systems that haven't been updated.
mistake: Patching isn't only for the finished product. The libraries, tools and operating systems the development team uses need patching too, and unpatched software is one of the study design's listed vulnerabilities.

front: Development versus testing versus production environment
back:
| | Development | Testing | Production |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| Used for | Writing and changing code | Checking changes before release | Running the live system |
| Used by | Developers | Testers | Staff and customers |
| Data it should hold | Made-up | Made-up or de-identified | Real, including personal information |

Kept separate, a change reaches production only after passing testing.
mistake: The production environment isn't where the software is produced. It is the live system that staff and customers rely on, holding real data; code is written in the development environment.

front: Why is threat modelling best started during design rather than after release?
back: A threat found in design can be removed by changing the design, which is far cheaper and quicker than reworking released code. Controls are then built in from the start rather than added later.
mistake: Threat modelling isn't a one-off check before release. It starts in design and is revisited whenever the system changes.

front: What does a data flow diagram contribute to threat modelling?
back: It shows where data enters and leaves the system, the processes that handle it and the stores that hold it. The team can then ask what could go wrong at each flow, process and store.

front: How are threats prioritised in threat modelling?
back: By risk: how likely each threat is to happen and how severe the harm would be. Threats that are both likely and harmful are mitigated first.
mistake: The most likely threat isn't automatically first. A less likely threat that would expose every customer's records can outrank a common threat that causes minor harm.

front: Threat mitigation
back: Applying controls that reduce a threat's likelihood or impact, or eliminate the threat, such as encrypting a data flow that could be intercepted, or requiring multi-factor authentication on accounts whose passwords could be guessed.

front: Why must each mitigation be tested once it has been built?
back: A planned control only helps if it was built correctly and actually blocks the threat. Testing it, for example by trying to open another user's record without permission, confirms that no identified threat has been left open.

front: Why should a threat model be updated when a feature is added?
back: A new feature can add data flows, data stores or ways into the system, and each can bring threats the original model never considered.

front: What is a security requirement? Give an example.
back: A requirement stating what the solution must do to protect its data and functions, which can be tested like any other requirement. Example: only pharmacists can view a customer's prescription history.

front: Threat modelling
back: A structured way of finding and dealing with the security threats to a system, begun during design and revisited whenever the system changes. The study design's principles are defining security requirements, identifying and mitigating threats, and confirming that the threats have been mitigated.
mistake: Threat modelling doesn't end once the security requirements are defined: the next principles are identifying and mitigating threats, then confirming they have been mitigated. Asked for one of these on the 2025 exam, 83% of students scored zero.

front: What is a criterion for evaluating the security of development practices?
back: A statement or question used to judge how well an organisation's software development practices protect its code, data and systems. It must be specific enough for evidence to show how far it is met, and may be set out as dot points. Examples: 'Every code repository account requires multi-factor authentication'; 'How consistently is each change reviewed before it is merged?'
mistake: A criterion isn't a vague goal such as 'the code is secure'. It must be specific enough that evidence can show whether it is met.

front: What makes a criterion for evaluating the security of development practices useful?
back:
It is:
- **specific**: it names the practice or security controls being judged
- **measurable**: evidence can show whether, or how far, it is met
- **relevant**: it is linked to a real risk to the organisation's code or data
- **realistic** for the organisation to meet
mistake: 'Developers follow good security' can't be tested. 'Access is removed on each leaver's last day' can be checked against records.

front: Security control versus security evaluation criterion
back:
| | Control | Criterion |
|:--|:--|:--|
| What it is | Hardware, software, equipment or a procedure that helps protect people, systems and data | A standard used to judge whether practices are secure |
| Example | Multi-factor authentication | All repository accounts require multi-factor authentication |
| Used when | Securing the practices | Evaluating the practices |
mistake: Listing a control ('MFA') doesn't answer a question that asks for a criterion. A criterion states the standard a practice must meet, so the practice can be judged against it.

front: State three criteria for evaluating how an organisation controls access to its code and data.
back:
Any three:
- each person has an individual account, with no shared logins
- access follows the principle of least privilege
- multi-factor authentication protects repositories and servers
- access is removed when staff leave
- access rights are reviewed regularly

front: State three criteria for evaluating how securely an organisation handles its source code.
back:
Any three:
- every change is reviewed by a second developer before it is merged
- no passwords or keys are stored in source code
- all code is kept in version control with a change history
- third-party libraries are updated when patches are released
- AI-generated code is reviewed and tested like any other code

front: State two criteria for evaluating how well an organisation separates its development, testing and production environments.
back:
Any two:
- development, testing and production run in separate environments
- developers can't change production directly; changes reach it only through a controlled release
- test environments use made-up or de-identified data, not live personal data
mistake: A separate test server isn't enough if it holds a copy of live customer data. Real personal information shouldn't be in development or test environments at all; they should use made-up or de-identified data.

front: What evidence could show whether the criterion 'access is removed on each staff member's last day' is met?
back: Compare staff departure dates in staff records with the dates their accounts were disabled in the access logs, and list any former staff accounts that are still active.
mistake: Asking managers whether access is removed gives their opinion, which may be wrong. Records and logs show what actually happened.

front: Evaluating the security of development practices judges the {{processes}} used to build software, such as access control and code review, not only the security of the {{finished solution}}.
back: An app can pass its security testing while the team that built it shares logins and stores passwords in its code.

front: Which three effectiveness measures does the study design give for development practices? Give a security criterion based on each.
back:
| Measure | Example criterion |
|:--|:--|
| Security controls in place | Every change is reviewed by a second developer before merging |
| Exposure to vulnerability and risk | No real customer data is held in development or test environments |
| Legal compliance | The team's handling of personal information meets APP 11 (Security of personal information) |

For data and information security strategies, the measures are confidentiality, integrity and availability.
mistake: Criteria don't only check that a control exists. A strong set also judges how exposed the practices leave code and data, and whether they meet the law that binds the organisation: APP 11 for an organisation the Privacy Act covers, or IPP 4 (Data security) for a Victorian public sector body.

front: What does the Privacy Act 1988 (Cwlth) regulate?
back: How personal information is collected, used, stored, disclosed and disposed of by Australian Government agencies and many private sector organisations. Its rules are set out in the Australian Privacy Principles.
mistake: The Privacy Act doesn't cover every organisation. Victorian public sector bodies, such as state departments and local councils, are covered by the Privacy and Data Protection Act 2014 (Vic) instead.

front: Privacy Act 1988 (Cwlth) versus Privacy and Data Protection Act 2014 (Vic)
back:
| | Privacy Act 1988 (Cwlth) | Privacy and Data Protection Act 2014 (Vic) |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Binds | Australian Government agencies and many private organisations | Victorian public sector bodies, such as departments and councils, and contractors bound by their contracts |
| Principles | Australian Privacy Principles | Information Privacy Principles |
mistake: Being based in Victoria doesn't put a private business under the Victorian Act. It binds the Victorian public sector, and a contractor only when its contract with a public sector body says so.

front: Health Records Act 2001 (Vic)
back: Victorian law that regulates how health information is collected, used, stored and disclosed by public and private sector organisations in Victoria, through its Health Privacy Principles.
mistake: It isn't limited to public hospitals. A private physiotherapy clinic in Victoria that keeps treatment notes must follow it too.

front: Why would a software development team apply the Essential Eight?
back: It gives a prioritised set of strategies for protecting the computers and servers the team uses to write, store and build code. Strategies such as patching, multi-factor authentication, restricting administrative privileges and regular backups make it much harder for attackers to break in, and help the team recover if they do.
mistake: The Essential Eight is guidance, not legislation. Most private organisations adopt it by choice, not because a law requires it.

front: Name the eight mitigation strategies in the Essential Eight.
back:
- Patch applications
- Patch operating systems
- Multi-factor authentication
- Restrict administrative privileges
- Application control
- Restrict Microsoft Office macros
- User application hardening
- Regular backups
mistake: Encryption, firewalls and antivirus software are useful controls, but none of them is one of the eight strategies.

front: Information Security Manual (ISM)
back: A cyber security framework published by the Australian Cyber Security Centre, part of the Australian Signals Directorate, that sets out principles and detailed controls, including guidelines for software development, for organisations to apply according to their risks.
mistake: The ISM isn't an Act or a fixed checklist. It is updated regularly, and each organisation chooses controls based on its own risks.

front: Legislation versus an industry framework
back:
| | Legislation | Industry framework |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Examples | Copyright Act 1968 (Cwlth), Privacy Act 1988 (Cwlth) | Essential Eight, Information Security Manual (ISM) |
| Made by | A parliament | A government agency or standards body |
| Compliance | Compulsory for those it covers; breaches can bring penalties | Voluntary guidelines, unless a contract or policy requires them |
mistake: Following a framework doesn't by itself meet legal obligations, and meeting the law doesn't mean every control a framework recommends is in place.

front: Under the Privacy Act 1988 (Cwlth), what must a covered organisation do after a data breach that is likely to cause serious harm?
back: Notify the individuals affected and the Office of the Australian Information Commissioner as soon as practicable, under the Notifiable Data Breaches scheme, so that people can act to protect themselves.
mistake: Fixing the vulnerability doesn't end the duty to notify. If serious harm is still likely, the people affected must be told.

front: Essential Eight
back: An industry framework from the Australian Cyber Security Centre: a prioritised set of eight mitigation strategies, such as patching applications, multi-factor authentication and regular backups, that makes an organisation's systems much harder to compromise and helps it recover after an attack. Organisations adopt it as guidance; it isn't legislation.

front: Multi-factor authentication
back: Authentication that requires two or more factors of different types, such as a password (something you know) plus a code sent to a phone (something you have), so a stolen password alone isn't enough to get in. It is one of the Essential Eight mitigation strategies.
mistake: A password and a PIN are both something you know, so together they aren't multi-factor authentication. The factors must be of different types.

front: What is the Copyright Act 1968 (Cwlth), what is its purpose, and what does it apply to?
back: A Commonwealth law that gives the owner of an original work exclusive rights, such as to copy, adapt (change), publish and share it online. Its purpose is to let creators control and benefit from their work, so others generally need the owner's permission, usually a licence. It applies to program code and documentation (as literary works), images, music, sound recordings and video.
mistake: Free to download doesn't mean free to reuse. Code, images and sounds found online are still protected, and their licence sets what you may do with them.

front: Which five Australian Privacy Principles (APPs) does the Unit 4 key knowledge list, and what does each mean for a program that handles personal information?
back:
- **APP 1** Open and transparent management of personal information: a clear, current privacy policy
- **APP 6** Use or disclosure of personal information: only for the purpose it was collected for, unless consent or another exception applies
- **APP 8** Cross-border disclosure of personal information: before sending it overseas, take reasonable steps so the recipient handles it as the APPs require
- **APP 9** Adoption, use or disclosure of government related identifiers: don't make a Medicare or driver licence number the customer ID
- **APP 11** Security of personal information: protect it, and destroy or de-identify it when no longer needed
mistake: APP 11 isn't only about keeping attackers out. Personal information that is no longer needed must be destroyed or de-identified, not kept just in case.

front: Which five Information Privacy Principles (IPPs) of the Privacy and Data Protection Act 2014 (Vic) does the Unit 4 key knowledge list, and what does each require?
back:
- **IPP 1** Collection: only what is necessary, collected fairly, telling people why
- **IPP 2** Use and disclosure: only for the purpose it was collected for, or a related one people would expect, unless an exception such as consent applies
- **IPP 4** Data security: protect it from misuse, loss and unauthorised access, and destroy or de-identify it when no longer needed
- **IPP 5** Openness: a clearly expressed policy on managing personal information, available on request
- **IPP 9** Transborder data flows: send it outside Victoria only if it will be protected to a similar standard, or an exception such as consent applies
mistake: The IPPs bind Victorian public sector bodies, such as councils and state departments. A private business follows the Privacy Act's APPs instead, when that Act covers it.

front: What are the four ISM Guidelines for Software Development, and what does each ask a development team to do?
back:
Purpose: to keep vulnerabilities and malicious code out of the software an organisation builds.

- **Development, testing, staging and production environments**: keep them separate, change code only in development, and keep production data in production unless another environment is secured to the same level
- **Authoritative source for software**: one trusted, access-controlled repository for all development work
- **Secure software development**: build security in from the design stage, for example by threat modelling
- **Software security testing**: test for security vulnerabilities before each release
mistake: Don't copy real customer data into development to make tests realistic: use made-up data. Production data belongs only in environments secured to the same level as production, which development environments rarely are.

front: Legal issue versus ethical issue
back:
| | Legal issue | Ethical issue |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Question | Does this break a law? | Does this go against moral standards, principles or what people reasonably expect? |
| Judged against | Legislation | Values such as honesty, fairness and care for others |
| Consequence | Penalties or legal action | Harm to the individuals or organisations affected, and loss of trust |
mistake: Legal doesn't mean ethical. No law stops a developer committing AI-generated code they haven't checked, yet doing so knowingly puts users at risk.

front: Why is over-reliance on AI-generated code an ethical issue for a developer?
back: The developer stays responsible for the code they commit. AI output can contain errors, security vulnerabilities or copied code, so using it unchecked puts users and their data at risk without their knowledge.
mistake: Using AI to write code isn't unethical in itself. The issue is relying on it without checking, and 'the AI wrote it' is no defence: the developer and organisation that release the code are accountable for its flaws.

front: Why is failing to acknowledge reused code an ethical issue?
back: It presents someone else's work as the developer's own, denies the original author credit, and hides where the code came from, so others can't check its licence or apply its security updates.
mistake: Acknowledgement matters even when a licence allows reuse. Permission to use code isn't permission to claim it.

front: Why is copying live customer data into a test environment an ethical issue?
back: Customers gave their data for one purpose and didn't agree to it being used for testing, and they don't know it has been copied. Using it anyway treats their information as the organisation's to use as it likes. Made-up or de-identified test data avoids this.
mistake: Realistic test data doesn't have to be real. Made-up records can match the format and range of live data.

front: A developer finds a serious vulnerability two days before a release deadline. What is the ethical course of action, and why?
back: Report it to the project manager with its likely impact, so the organisation can fix it or delay the release. Hiding it to meet the deadline puts the organisation's convenience ahead of users' safety.
mistake: Releasing on time and fixing it 'in the next update' without telling anyone leaves users exposed in the meantime, without their knowledge.

front: An ethical issue arises when a development decision conflicts with {{moral standards}}, principles or what people reasonably expect, and could affect individuals or organisations, even when {{no law is broken}}.
back: Ethics asks whether a choice is right for everyone it affects, such as users, clients, colleagues, the organisation and the public, not only whether it is legal.

front: Why is collecting more personal data than a program needs an ethical issue?
back: Every extra item stored adds to the harm if the data is exposed, and users may not expect or agree to it being kept. Collecting only what the program needs limits both problems.
mistake: 'We might need it later' isn't a reason to collect data. Data that is never collected can't be exposed.

front: Why is hiding a data breach from the people affected an ethical issue?
back: Without being told, people can't protect themselves, for example by changing passwords or watching their accounts. Hiding the breach also misleads them and damages their trust in the organisation.
mistake: Hiding a breach isn't only an ethical issue. When serious harm is likely, organisations covered by the Privacy Act 1988 (Cwlth) must notify the people affected.

front: Apart from failing to acknowledge reused code, which development practices raise intellectual property issues?
back:
- Using pirated (unlicensed) software or development tools
- Sharing or selling a program or its code without the owner's permission
- Ignoring the conditions of an open-source licence
- Reverse engineering proprietary software to copy or change its code
- Taking code owned by an employer or client to reuse elsewhere

Each uses someone's work without permission or outside the terms they allow, and can cost them income.
mistake: Crediting the author doesn't make every use acceptable. Using or sharing code without the owner's permission, or outside its licence, is still wrong and can infringe copyright.

front: How does least privilege limit the damage when a developer's account is stolen?
back: The attacker can do only what that account was allowed to do. If the developer's account reaches only the development and test systems, the attacker can't change production or read live customer data through it.
mistake: Least privilege doesn't stop an account being stolen; it limits what a stolen account can do. Multi-factor authentication makes theft harder, so the two work together.

front: Reducing a risk versus eliminating a risk
back:
| | Reduce | Eliminate |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Effect | Lowers the likelihood or the impact | Removes the threat or vulnerability entirely |
| Example | Encrypting stored card numbers | No longer storing card numbers at all |
mistake: Most measures reduce risk rather than remove it. Encrypted data can still be exposed if the key is stolen.

front: How does separating development, testing and production environments reduce risk?
back: Unfinished or faulty code can't directly affect the live system, developers don't need access to live data, and an attacker who breaks into the development environment doesn't automatically reach production.
mistake: Separation only works if changes reach production through a controlled release. A developer who can still edit production directly defeats it.

front: A database password is hard-coded in source code stored in the team's repository. What measures remove this risk?
back: Change the password, because the old one remains in the version history, and store credentials outside the code, in a protected configuration file or secrets store that only authorised systems can read.
mistake: Moving the password into a configuration file doesn't help if that file is committed to the repository too. Files that hold secrets must be kept out of version control.

front: Backups don't stop an attack, but they reduce its {{impact}} by letting code and data be {{restored}}, provided restores are {{tested}} regularly.
back: An untested backup may be incomplete or unreadable. Keeping one copy offline, disconnected from the network, stops ransomware from encrypting it too.

front: Why should an organisation layer several security measures rather than rely on one?
back: If one measure fails or is bypassed, the others still protect the code and data. Multi-factor authentication, least privilege, code review and tested backups each cover gaps the others leave. This approach is often called defence in depth.
mistake: A strong password isn't enough on its own. Once it is phished, multi-factor authentication stops it working alone, and least privilege limits what an attacker can reach.

front: Give two physical measures that protect a development team's code and data.
back:
Any two:
- servers kept in a locked room with logged swipe-card access
- backup drives stored in a locked, fire-resistant safe away from the main office
- visitors signed in and escorted through development areas
- old drives physically destroyed before disposal
mistake: Passwords and encryption are software measures. Physical measures control who can reach the equipment itself.

front: Least privilege
back: The security principle that each user, program or process gets only the access rights its duties require, and no administrator rights unless they are essential. It underpins robust identity and access management, and it limits what a careless, dishonest or stolen account can do.
mistake: Least privilege applies to developers too. A developer who changes code in the development environment doesn't need access to production systems or live customer data.

front: What makes a recommendation to improve an organisation's development practices effective?
back:
It:
- states a specific action
- is linked to a weakness found in that organisation
- explains how the action reduces the risk
- is realistic for the organisation's budget, skills and size
mistake: 'Improve security' isn't a recommendation. Say what to change, where, and which risk it reduces.

front: Finding versus recommendation
back:
| | Finding | Recommendation |
|:--|:--|:--|
| States | What is wrong now | What should change, and why |
| Example | Developers share one administrator login | Give each developer an individual account with only the rights they need, so actions can be traced and misuse limited |
mistake: Restating the problem ('there is no code review') isn't a recommendation. Turn it into an action and state its benefit.

front: How should an organisation prioritise several security recommendations?
back: By the risk each one addresses, as a risk management plan does: rate each weakness by its likelihood and impact, and deal first with the highest. Among serious risks, favour quick, low-cost fixes, such as turning on multi-factor authentication that is already available.
mistake: The most expensive recommendation isn't automatically the most important. A free setting change can remove a serious risk.

front: What should a recommendation to introduce mandatory code review specify?
back: That every change is approved by a developer other than its author before it is merged, that the repository blocks unapproved merges, what reviewers check (such as secrets, validation and AI-generated code), and which risk this reduces.
mistake: Code review is a security control, not a strategy. In 2025, describing a control when the question asked for a strategy to improve secure development practice earned no marks; give developer training, onboarding/induction or a risk management plan instead.

front: When a question asks you to {{recommend}}, choose a course of action and give a {{reason}} that links it to the scenario.
back: A list of options with no choice made, or a choice with no reason, doesn't do what the command term asks. If the question asks for two recommendations, give two different ones, each with its own reason: the same idea reworded scores only once.
mistake: Listing several options without choosing between them doesn't answer a 'recommend' question. Commit to a choice and give its reason.

front: Why should a recommendation consider its effect on the development team's work?
back: Measures that slow work too much are often bypassed, such as sharing one login to avoid multi-factor authentication prompts. A practical measure that staff actually follow protects more than a stricter one they work around.
mistake: The most secure option isn't always the best recommendation. It must suit the organisation's size, budget and way of working.

front: State four rules a development team could set for its use of AI coding assistants.
back: AI-generated code is reviewed and tested like any other code, developers must understand code before committing it, AI use is recorded, and no confidential code or personal data is entered into public AI tools.

front: How can an organisation check whether a recommendation has improved its development practices?
back: Evaluate the practices again against the same criteria used before the change, with the same kinds of evidence, and compare the results, for example the number of accounts holding administrator rights they don't need.

front: Which two strategies for improving the security of software development practices does the study design list?
back:
- Onboarding/induction practices and developer training focused on secure development
- Development of risk management plans

Each improves how the whole team works. Security controls, such as code review, encryption and separated environments, are a separate list.
mistake: A security control, such as code review or encryption, isn't a strategy. In 2025, answers that described a security control when a strategy was asked for earned no marks.

front: A risk management plan lists the potential {{risks}} to a project, rates each one's {{likelihood}} and {{impact}}, and proposes {{security controls}} to reduce them.
back: The ratings show which risks to deal with first. Developing the plan is one of the study design's strategies for improving secure development practices; the controls it proposes are not strategies in their own right.
mistake: A list of risks on its own isn't a risk management plan. Without likelihood and impact ratings and a proposed control for each risk, it can't show what to fix first or how.

front: Onboarding/induction and developer training versus a risk management plan
back:
| | Onboarding/induction and training | Risk management plan |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Advantage | Every developer learns secure habits from the start, so fewer weaknesses are created | Ranks risks by likelihood and impact, so time and money go to the most serious first |
| Disadvantage | Costs time and money, and must be repeated as staff and threats change | Takes effort to prepare, and goes out of date unless it is reviewed |
